blocks.text: Continued pretraining takes an already pretrained base model and further trains it on a large, raw, unlabeled text corpus from a specific domain, extending the model general knowledge into that domain before any of the task-specific fine-tuning methods covered elsewhere in this course are applied.

This topic covers how continued pretraining differs from supervised fine-tuning in both objective and data needs, where it fits in a full training pipeline, and the domain adaptation use cases it is best suited for.
1. What Continued Pretraining Does

blocks.alt: A pretrained base model goes through continued pretraining, producing a domain adapted model

blocks.text: Continued pretraining resumes the same next-token prediction objective a model originally learned during its initial pretraining, but now applied to a new corpus of text, typically from a specific domain, deepening the model general knowledge of that domain vocabulary, style, and content before any task-specific training happens.
2. Continued Pretraining vs Supervised Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Supervised fine-tuning uses labeled instruction pairs while continued pretraining uses a next token objective on raw text

blocks.text: Supervised fine-tuning, covered in an earlier module, trains on labeled instruction and response pairs, teaching a model to follow specific task formats, continued pretraining instead uses the same unsupervised next-token prediction objective as original pretraining, applied to raw, unlabeled domain text, a fundamentally different training signal.
3. No Labels Needed

blocks.alt: A raw domain text corpus needs no labels

blocks.text: Because continued pretraining uses the same self-supervised objective as original pretraining, it needs only raw domain text, legal documents, medical literature, internal company documentation, with no labeling or annotation effort required, a meaningfully lower data preparation cost than supervised fine-tuning.
4. Data Volume Requirements

blocks.alt: Continued pretraining needs a large corpus while SFT needs far less data

blocks.text: Continued pretraining generally needs a substantially larger volume of text than supervised fine-tuning to meaningfully shift a model knowledge, since it is teaching broad domain familiarity rather than a specific narrow behavior, this data volume difference is a key practical planning consideration.

blocks.text: 5. Where Continued Pretraining Fits in the Pipeline

blocks.alt: Original pretraining is followed by continued pretraining, then SFT, then alignment

blocks.text: Continued pretraining typically happens after original pretraining but before the supervised fine-tuning and alignment stages covered throughout this course, establishing broad domain knowledge first so that the subsequent task-specific training stages have a stronger foundation to build on.
6. The Catastrophic Forgetting Risk

blocks.alt: A too high learning rate leads to catastrophic forgetting

blocks.text: Continued pretraining with too aggressive a learning rate risks catastrophic forgetting, covered in earlier modules, where the model general capabilities degrade as it over-adapts to the new domain corpus, using a conservative learning rate and monitoring general benchmark performance, covered in an earlier topic, throughout continued pretraining helps guard against this.

blocks.title: This is the same forgetting risk covered elsewhere, applied at a different training stage
blocks.content: Catastrophic forgetting is a recurring concern across this course, in continued pretraining specifically, the risk is losing broad general knowledge in exchange for domain depth, a tradeoff worth actively monitoring rather than assuming will not happen.

blocks.text: 7. Domain Adaptation Use Cases

blocks.alt: A general domain model is compared against a continued pretrained model for legal, medical, or scientific domains

blocks.text: Continued pretraining is particularly valuable for specialized domains with distinctive vocabulary and content patterns quite different from general web text, legal, medical, and scientific domains being common examples, where a general purpose base model genuinely lacks deep familiarity that continued pretraining on in-domain text can provide.
8. Continued Pretraining vs Domain and Task Adaptive Pretraining

Continued pretraining as covered here is the general version of this idea, the following two topics, Domain Adaptive Pretraining and Task Adaptive Pretraining, cover two more specifically scoped variants of the same underlying technique, tailored to a domain corpus versus a task-specific corpus respectively.
9. Cost Considerations

Because continued pretraining needs both a large corpus and meaningful compute to process it, connecting to the training infrastructure considerations covered in earlier modules, it represents a more expensive investment than supervised fine-tuning alone, worth undertaking specifically when a domain genuinely requires knowledge a general base model lacks, rather than as a default first step.
Worked Example

A team building a legal document assistant finds their general-purpose base model frequently misunderstands specialized legal terminology and citation formats, even after supervised fine-tuning on legal instruction examples.

They add a continued pretraining stage on a large corpus of raw legal text before their existing supervised fine-tuning pipeline, using a conservative learning rate and monitoring general benchmark scores throughout to catch any forgetting, the resulting model shows noticeably better legal terminology handling in the subsequent fine-tuning and evaluation stages than their previous general-purpose starting point did.
Common Mistakes

items: Using too aggressive a learning rate during continued pretraining, risking catastrophic forgetting of general capability
Attempting continued pretraining with too small a domain corpus to meaningfully shift model knowledge
Skipping continued pretraining for a domain that genuinely needs it and relying on supervised fine-tuning alone
Not monitoring general benchmark performance throughout continued pretraining to catch forgetting early

blocks.text: Practice

For a specialized domain you are familiar with, legal, medical, or another technical field, assess whether a general purpose model would likely benefit from continued pretraining on in-domain text before supervised fine-tuning, and explain what specific terminology or content gaps would justify that investment.
Key Takeaway

Continued pretraining extends a base model general knowledge into a specific domain using the same self-supervised next-token objective as original pretraining, applied to a large raw text corpus with no labeling needed, typically happening before supervised fine-tuning and alignment stages, and it requires careful learning rate management to avoid catastrophic forgetting of general capability while gaining domain depth.
